scenes.narration: Meet Maya. She trains artificial intelligence in a lab in Montreal, and this morning her phone won't stop buzzing. Headline after headline says the same thing. Canada's economy is crashing. Then a message from California. A big AI lab wants her. Bigger paycheck, bigger computers, more sunshine. Pack your bags, it says. Meanwhile, far to the south, in the desert, somebody else is packing too. This is Whirr. Whirr is a data center, and Whirr is overheating. Its fans are screaming, its power bill keeps climbing, and it needs a new home. Maya is thinking of moving south. Whirr is thinking of moving north. One of them has read the map wrong. So which is it? Is Canada losing the AI boom, or could it be the biggest winner of all?

scenes.narration: To be fair, the bad news is real. Back in the spring of twenty twenty-five, American tariffs hit Canadian cars and machinery, exports fell, and the economy actually shrank. Maya's uncle sells car parts. He stopped smiling at the news. The headlines did the math. Crash.

But crashes don't usually bounce. This year the economy grew again, and the Bank of Canada expects more growth ahead, even if new tariffs slow things down this winter. That's a forecast, not a promise. Still, it's not the picture on Maya's phone.

scenes.narration: Let me draw what an AI factory needs. Start with a plug: huge amounts of electricity, all day and all night. Then a fridge: every chip turns power into heat, and the heat has to go somewhere. Then a mine: chips, cables and batteries are made of metal. And finally, a brain: people who know how to build the models. Most countries are strong in a couple of these. Very few have the whole list.

scenes.narration: Whirr heads north first, following the power lines. They lead out of the mountains and down the rivers, to dams the size of small towns. Of all its electricity, Canada makes about six of every ten kilowatt hours from falling water. Whirr has never seen anything like it.

keyframes.cue: They lead out of the mountains

scenes.narration: That makes Canada the third-biggest hydropower maker on the planet. Whirr does a little dance. Clean, steady, and already built.

In Quebec, the power is famous for being cheap. A big factory there pays less than a quarter of what the same factory would pay in Boston. We told that story in Could Cheap Electricity Become the New Oil? Whirr starts unpacking.

Then comes the twist. Hydro-Québec says its days of surplus power are over. Big new users now need the government's permission, and the price it has proposed for data centers is more than double what big industry pays today. It's still a proposal, still under review. Whirr stops unpacking.

scenes.narration: Still, the north has one gift nobody has to build. Whirr steps outside, and for the first time in ages, its fans slow down. In the desert, a data center spends a fortune on air conditioning. Up here, the cold air does a lot of that work for free. Whirr sighs. Ahhh.

One Quebec operator says it can cool its servers with outside air most of the year. That's its own claim, and it depends on how a building is designed. But the idea is simple. The cold is a giant, natural fridge.

And the heat that comes out of the servers doesn't have to be wasted. In Kamloops, British Columbia, the phone company Bell plans an AI data center at a university that will pipe its leftover heat into the campus buildings. The servers keep the students warm.

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, Maya goes home for the weekend, to Sudbury, Ontario, where her dad, Luc, works at a nickel mine. He has heard about California. You know what's inside those AI computers? he asks. Rocks. Our rocks.

He's not wrong. Copper for the wires. Nickel, lithium and graphite for the batteries. Uranium for the nuclear plants that could power the data centers. Canada's government keeps an official list of minerals the modern economy can't do without. There are thirty-four on it, and Canada mines many of them.
In uranium, Canada is the world's second-biggest producer. Luc grins. Rocks, he says again.

But here's the catch with rocks. They're slow. Around the world, a big new mine has taken more than sixteen years, on average, to go from discovery to the first truckload of ore. By then, Maya's AI models would be ancient history.

Ottawa has set up a Major Projects Office to speed up approvals. One copper and zinc mine in Saskatchewan was referred to it and started producing less than a year later, although it was already mostly built. Fast for a mine. Whether that becomes normal is the real test.

scenes.narration: Back in Montreal, Maya walks into her lab, and you can see why California wants her. Some of the big ideas behind today's AI grew up right here, in Canadian universities, when most of the world had given up on them.

scenes.narration: In Toronto, Geoffrey Hinton spent decades on artificial neural networks, when much of the field thought they were a dead end. In twenty twenty-four, that work helped earn him the Nobel Prize in Physics.
In Montreal, Yoshua Bengio founded the lab that grew into Mila, which describes itself as the world's largest academic research center for deep learning. Maya's lab is just down the street.
Canada was also the first country in the world to launch a national AI strategy. And now it's paying to build a giant AI supercomputer of its own, owned in Canada.

scenes.narration: So where's the problem? Follow Maya's classmates. Most science and tech graduates do stay in Canada, Statistics Canada finds. But the stars get the biggest offers, and many of those come from American companies with deeper pockets. Promising Canadian startups often find their biggest buyers, and their biggest checks, south of the border. Maya's phone buzzes. The recruiter again. Decided yet? Not yet.

scenes.narration: Let me draw Canada's talent pipeline. Students go in here, at the universities. They come out as researchers, and then as founders. But look at this pipe. There's a leak, and it points south: higher pay, bigger computers, bigger funding. Canada doesn't need to stop the water. It needs to give it reasons to stay: computers to work on at home, and companies big enough to grow up here.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the biggest catch of all. Canada's best customer is also its biggest risk. Of every dollar of goods Canada sells abroad, nearly three of every four dollars go to the United States. When Washington adds tariffs, Canada feels it first.

AI could change that list. Electricity turned into computing doesn't ride on trucks. It travels through cables. That could be a new kind of export, but only if Canada builds the data centers, and only if someone at home owns the companies that use them.

keyframes.cue: That could be a new kind of export
keyframes.label: items[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: So here's the scorecard. Power: plenty, but the cheap part is taken, and new dams and lines take years. Cold: free. Metals: in the ground, but slow to dig up. Brains: world class, but tempted south. And next door, a giant neighbor that can slow everything down with a tariff.

So, could Canada be the biggest winner of the AI boom? It has something rare: the whole shopping list, in one country. Power, cold, metals and brains. Most countries would trade a lot for that. But having the list isn't the same as winning. Canada wins only if it builds: power lines, mines, data centers, and companies that grow up at home instead of moving away.

scenes.narration: And that crash everyone talks about? It's real for some industries, like the car parts hit by tariffs. But the AI boom is betting on a different Canada. The one behind the dams, under the snow, and inside the labs.

Back in Montreal, Maya opens the California offer one more time. Then she looks out the window. Across the street, a new building is going up, and a friendly data center waves at her. It's Whirr. I moved in, it says. Your turn. Maya types her answer. Ask me again next year. For now, I'm staying.
